seriesTitle: The Lantern Mender of Pell Street
title: A Wheel Short of Done
blurb: Ada cannot say what she saw in the Provost's lantern, so she sends Emrys to the records. Then the clock tower, and a lantern far above her tier.

blocks.text: "You saw something in the Provost's lantern."
Emrys said it very quietly. That was how Ada knew how angry he was.
Rain ticked on the shop window. On the bench behind her the old unlit lantern sat where it always sat.
"You came out of that hall the colour of paper, and you have not looked at me once since. You know who the Breaker is." Quieter still. "Say it."
Ada opened her mouth.
At the corner of her eye, over the unlit lantern, the readout flared. Not gold. Red. The red of a breaker about to trip.
Exile into the fog. Below the wick.
She closed her mouth.

Emrys waited. The rain waited. Then he put his spectacles back on, which he only did when he had finished looking at someone, and walked out. The shop bell rang behind him like something small being dropped.

At first bell there were buns on the step in their twist of paper, still warm, and Hester's humming going away down Pell Street with her ladder. Ada took the buns in and did not eat them. She took the brown wrapping paper out of the drawer instead and wrote, in pencil, under the third line:
4. His name. The man in the van.
She was still looking at it when the bell went again.
Emrys stood in the doorway with his coat buttoned to the throat. He had not slept either. He had the look of a man who had written something down several times and crossed it out.
"I asked you to walk into the fog," he said. "For a name. That was, for the record, the worst thing I have said to anyone in this office, or out of it, which is not a large field, but still."
"You were angry."
"I was frightened. They look the same on me." He glanced at the list on the bench, and away from it, politely, as if she were undressed. "Four."
"Four."
He did not ask what it cost. She almost wished he would.
"Emrys. In the hall, when the bar filled, I saw an—"
Red. Hard, at the edge of her sight, over the bench.
She stopped. Counted two. Started somewhere else.
"The Provost's hall writes things down. Doesn't it? Not lanterns. Paper."
He blinked. "Everything. Minutes, orders, the bell roster, the key book. It is a hall that would minute its own fire."
"And anyone can read it?"
"Any resident, under the charter, between third bell and sixth." A pause. "I am a resident."
"What does it say about Flood Night?"
He looked at her for a long moment. Then he went to fetch his umbrella.

The record room was at the back of the Provost's hall, behind a door that stuck. Inside it was colder than the hall, which Ada had not thought possible. Shelves of ledgers, spine to spine. The drip of a gutter somewhere outside. Emrys's pencil, tapping the shelf as he read the spines.
"Minutes," he said. "Proclamations. Wreck and salvage."
"Who signs for things," said Ada. "At night. If somebody takes something out of here at night."
The pencil stopped.
He took down a thin book bound in green cloth. KEYS, on the spine, in gold that had mostly gone. He did not have to look for the page. The ink on that page was darker, and there was more of it.

"Bridge house, returned," he read. "Bell tower, out, returned. Lower sluice house." He stopped. "Out at ninth bell. Signed, R. Harrow." His finger moved along the line. "Returned. No time given. Nobody signed it back in."
The gutter dripped.
"The Provost does not carry keys," Emrys said. "She has people for keys. Why would she want the sluice house, on that night, herself?"
Ada said nothing.

He turned round. "You asked me for the key book. Not the minutes, not the roll of the drowned. The key book. And then you asked me who signs for things at night." His voice went down and down. "You knew where to look."
"I can't—"
"No. I know. I entered it in the margin myself." He closed the book very gently. "For the record, that is worse. I would almost rather you were lying."

Odile's front room smelled of stove and wet wool. Rain on the window. The green dress on its dummy, one sleeve on. On the hearth shelf, in the clean square, Ines's lantern burned small and low, the ragged gap in its glass turned to the wall.
Four cups on the table. Odile poured all four and pushed one at the empty chair without seeming to notice she had done it.

"The Provost," said Odile, around two pins. "Oh, I've seen the Provost. The night you did Ines. I came home the long way, over the bridge, with her in my shawl, and who's standing at the bottom of Cutter's Row at that hour, by the towpath steps, like she's waiting for a ferry that doesn't—"
"Doesn't run at night," said Emrys.
"Doesn't exist," said Odile, which was not what she had been going to say either. "Gloves and all. She's always got the gloves on. You'd think she was born in them and the midwife just—"
"Buttoned them," said Ada.
"Smacked her," said Odile. "But yes."
Emrys had a pencil out. He did not write in the Register. He wrote on the back of Hester's bun paper, which Ada had in her pocket, flattened on Odile's table between the cups.
1. Gloves. Never off. 2. Sluice house key, Flood Night. Not returned in her hand. 3. Cutter's Row, the night of the twelfth line.
"There's a fourth," said Ada. "The old Mender wrote it in the ledger. Hot glass marks the hand that breaks it. Silver, and for life."
That was ink on a page, not a secret. The readout stayed dark.
Emrys wrote it down. "Nobody in Morrow Quay has seen the Provost's palms in ten years."
"Then that's where you test," said Ada.

He looked at her over his spectacles, and for a moment it was the look from the towpath, the one that said *I'll want to see how you do that again*. Something in her chest that had been clamped since first bell let go a quarter turn.
It was a good list. It was a tidy list. It pointed one way.
And there was a line Ada could not give him, in a gloved hand on a dead night: *Whose watch?* She did not know what it meant for the list. She only knew she was holding it, and he was not.
The stairs in the clock tower were iron and went round and round. At the top, wind sang through the louvres, and somewhere in the dark a man was tapping. Three short, one long. Three short, one long.
"Mender," said Tobias, without turning round. "You're late."
"I didn't say I was coming."
"Still late."
The clock filled the room: wheels on wheels, brass gone brown, every tooth clean. On his bench lay a single wheel, bright as a coin. Sixty teeth.
"That's the last," said Tobias. "Goes in tonight. By lamplight. Always has."

Behind the clock face, where light should come through the numbers, hung a lantern the size of a rain barrel. Its glass was black. Not dirty. Dark, the way a house is dark when everyone in it has gone.
The readout came up over it before she asked. A word she had never seen, so bright it hurt to look at.
HEART.
Unknown rating. Test before you touch.

Ada knew, somewhere under the knowing, that the word was a long way above her. She also knew the clock was one wheel from done and the road home was on the other side of this glass, and asking would take longer.
She laid her palm flat on it, the way you check a radiator.
Heat, all at once, like grabbing a kettle by the side. She snatched her hand back and the other one with it, and swore at the lantern, and then again, at the lantern, for good measure.
Both palms red. Hot red, throbbing to the wrist.
She had done this once before. Overridden the warning because the warning was slow. She did not think about when.
"Fool thing to do," said Tobias, and put her hands in a bucket of cold water before she could argue. "Old one came down those stairs with hands like that, once. Red by supper. Gone by morning."
Red, Ada thought. Not silver. It would heal by tomorrow. Silver never did.
"What is it?"

"Great Lantern. What the town remembers together." He tapped the bench. Three short, one long. "Went dark on Flood Night. Dark, she won't run. Not for me, not for anyone. And while she won't run, the fog road won't open."
"Then why finish her?"
He looked at the bright wheel for a long time.
"Clock's got to be ready," he said. "Light comes back, she'll want to go. Wouldn't do to keep her waiting."
Ada took her hands out of the water. They stung in the cold air.
"Tobias. The woman. The one you see every night." He went still. "I know her name. It's yours to hear if you want it. Not mine to tell anyone else."
The wind sang through the louvres.
"Go on, then."
"Ines Fane. Odile's sister. Her twin."
The tapping stopped.

"Fane," he said. "Got her name back the other night, same as the whole Quay. Never put it to the face. Thought the face was Odile's, and Odile's alive, so I thought I'd gone soft." His jaw worked. "Ten years I've crossed the square when Odile Fane comes. Couldn't look at her. Told myself it was the chatter." He put his big hand flat on the clock frame, as if it might go somewhere. "Ines."
At the market the lamps were not up yet, and the chestnut man was shouting about chestnuts as if anyone had forgotten. Hester was there with her basket, humming, gloves on, cutting pie.
Tobias walked into the middle of it all and stopped.

"Hear this," he said, louder than Ada had known he could. Stalls went quiet, one by one. "Clock's a wheel off. Wheel goes in tonight. And when she runs, I'm having the Mender look proper at my Flood Night. What's in my lantern. I want to know what I did."
Somewhere behind Ada, the humming stopped.
"Pie!" said Hester, bright as a bell. "Who's for pie, my ducks? Pork and apple, still hot. Tobias, love, you'll have a slice, you're all bones—"
She went round the stalls with the knife and the dish, pressing pie on people who had not asked, and nobody said anything else about Flood Night.
Tobias stopped at Ada's elbow on his way out. He looked at her red hands.
"Ninth bell," he said. "My shop, under the tower. Need steady hands for the last wheel." A grunt. "Steadier than those."
Ninth bell came across the water, deep and slow.
The door of the clock shop under the tower stood open. No lamp lit inside. No tapping.
"Tobias?"
Ada stepped in. Her hands still stung. Something crunched under her boot.
Glass. Curved glass, all across the bench, fingernail-sized, and when she touched one with a finger that still hurt, it was warm.
The bright wheel lay beside it. Sixty teeth.
"Ada?" Odile, at the door, her green umbrella dripping. "What on earth are you doing in old empty? That shop's been empty since—well. Since ever. Hasn't it? Nobody's had it since—"
"Tobias Penhallow," said Ada.
Odile smiled at her, kind and puzzled.
"Who?"
Ada looked at the glass on the bench. A lantern was memory, not breath. The rules said a smashed lantern meant forgotten, alive or dead. They did not say dead.
She was the only person left in Morrow Quay who remembered Tobias Penhallow. And somewhere out in the dark, with nobody left to know his name, he was still alive.
